stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Walk through **Les Buissonnets** in Lisieux and see Thérèse’s actual childhood bedroom, toys, and the quiet garden bench where she gazed up at the night sky spotting the **"T" formed by Orion’s stars** and smiling that her name was written in heaven!

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Crowning the green hills of Lisieux, the magnificent **Basilica of St. Thérèse** welcomes nearly **1 million pilgrims a year**—and even **astronauts** have carried St. Thérèse’s relics aboard space shuttle missions!

stops.didYouKnowHighlight: St. Padre Pio, St. John Bosco, and St. Francis de Sales all gave the same joyful everyday tip: **when heading into a tough meeting or misunderstanding, quietly ask your Guardian Angel to go ahead and speak with the other person’s Guardian Angel!**

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today in Assisi (Province of Perugia in Umbria, central Italy), pilgrims walk the medieval pink-limestone streets from the Piazza del Vescovado—where Francis renounced his inheritance—to the two-story Papal Basilica of San Francesco, where Giotto’s frescoes and Francis’s stone crypt tomb rest.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Before St. Francis was buried here in 1230, the western promontory of Assisi was called "Colle d’Inferno" (Hill of Hell) because criminals were executed there. Pope Gregory IX renamed it "Colle del Paradiso" (Hill of Paradise) when laying the basilica’s foundation stone!
stops.saintQuote: “Lord, make me an instrument of Your peace; where there is hatred, let me sow love.”

detectiveClues.clueText: Look to central Italy between Rome and Florence, in the region of Umbria. Built from the rose-tinted limestone of Mount Subasio, this terraced town overlooks the fertile Spoleto Valley.

detectiveClues.headline: From "Hill of Hell" to "Hill of Paradise" & Giotto’s 28 Frescoes
detectiveClues.clueText: At the western tip of this town rises a two-level Papal Basilica containing 28 masterpieces by Giotto and a sunken rock crypt holding the saint’s rough stone sarcophagus flanked by Brothers Leo, Rufino, Masseo, and Angelo!

detectiveClues.headline: Handing Back His Fine Clothes in the Bishop’s Square (1206)
detectiveClues.clueText: Nicknamed "Francesco" ("The Little Frenchman") by his silk-merchant father Pietro, the former troubadour and prisoner-of-war publicly returned his purse and velvet garments in the bishop’s courtyard here in 1206.

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today, a 15-minute walk down a steep cobbled footpath through olive groves outside Porta Nuova in Assisi leads to the untouched stone Sanctuary of San Damiano, where St. Clare lived for 41 years and where St. Francis composed the Canticle of the Sun.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: When the painted wooden Byzantine crucifix at San Damiano said, "Francis, go and repair My house, which as you see is falling into ruin," literal-minded young Francis immediately started begging for actual stones and mortar in the streets to patch the chapel’s crumbling walls with his own hands!
stops.saintQuote: “Praised be You, my Lord, with all Your creatures, especially Sir Brother Sun, who is the day and through whom You give us light.”

detectiveClues.headline: A Rustic 12th-Century Stone Sanctuary in the Olive Groves Below Assisi
detectiveClues.clueText: Look to the southern olive slopes just below the medieval walls of Assisi in Umbria, Italy. This three-arched stone convent remains virtually unchanged since the 13th century.

detectiveClues.headline: Where Blind & Ailing Francis Composed the First Poem in Italian Literature
detectiveClues.clueText: Resting in a reed hut on the garden terrace here in 1225 while nearly blind, Francis composed "The Canticle of the Creatures" (Brother Sun, Sister Moon)—the earliest known masterpiece written in the vernacular Italian language!

detectiveClues.headline: "Francis, Go and Repair My House" (1205)
detectiveClues.clueText: Kneeling inside this crumbling country chapel in 1205, Francis heard the painted Byzantine icon cross speak three times, and later welcomed St. Clare and her sisters to live here for over four decades.

stops.title: Brother Wolf & The Peace Pact of Gubbio

stops.eraLabel: c. 1206 – 1220 AD · Taming the Fierce Wolf
stops.imageCaption: Statue of St. Francis and Brother Wolf before the medieval stone church in the Apennine mountain town of Gubbio, Umbria, Italy.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today in the medieval stone town of Gubbio (40 km north of Assisi on the slopes of Mount Ingino in northern Umbria, Italy), visitors see the Church of San Francesco della Pace ("Chiesa della Vittorina")—where the wolf’s skull and stone sarcophagus are kept—and the Basilica of San Francesco.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: After walking out of Assisi naked in 1206, Gubbio was the very first town Francis walked to, where his old friend Federico Spadalunga gave him his first rough gray-brown tunic. And in 1872, masons renovating the Church of San Francesco della Pace actually unearthed a large medieval wolf skeleton buried beneath the threshold!
stops.saintQuote: “Come here, Brother Wolf! I command you in the name of Christ that you do no harm to me or to anyone else.”

stops.detectiveCaseTitle: Case #3 · The Mountain Town of the Tamed Apennine Wolf
stops.detectiveLeadPrompt: Read the 3 clues below, then spin the 3D Globe to the northern Umbrian mountain town where Francis shook paws with "Brother Wolf."

detectiveClues.headline: A Perfectly Preserved Medieval Stone Town on Mount Ingino in Northern Umbria
detectiveClues.clueText: Look 40 km north of Assisi into the Umbrian Apennines. Famous for its hanging Palazzo dei Consoli and the annual Corsa dei Ceri race, this town is linked to Assisi by the "Sentiero Francescano della Pace" hiking trail.

detectiveClues.headline: The Medieval Wolf Skeleton Discovered Under the Church Floor in 1872
detectiveClues.clueText: Inside this town’s Church of San Francesco della Pace rests a carved stone lid over the skeleton of a large Apennine wolf discovered during 1872 renovations—kept for two peaceful years fed by the townsfolk!

detectiveClues.headline: "Brother Wolf, Give Me Your Pledge of Peace" (Fioretti Ch. 21)
detectiveClues.clueText: When a ravenous wolf terrorized this town, Francis walked out unarmed beyond the city gates, made the Sign of the Cross, and brokered a peace treaty in which the wolf placed its right paw in Francis’s hand.

stops.title: The Cliffside Grotto & The World’s First Christmas Nativity
stops.subtitle: Explore the cliff-clinging Sanctuary of Greccio above the Rieti Valley
stops.eraLabel: Christmas Eve, 1223 AD · First Living Crèche
stops.imageCaption: Franciscan Sanctuary of Greccio built into the limestone cliffside overlooking the Rieti Valley in Lazio, Italy, birthplace of the Christmas Nativity scene.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today at the Sanctuary of Greccio (perched at 638 meters altitude on a sheer rock cliff in the Province of Rieti, northern Lazio, Italy), pilgrims enter the original rock Cave of the Nativity (Cappella del Presepio) and visit an international museum of Christmas Nativity scenes from around the world.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Every Christmas Nativity scene (presepio / crèche) in the world today—under Christmas trees, in churches, and on town squares—traces its origin to December 24, 1223, when Francis asked his friend Giovanni Velita of Greccio to bring a real manger filled with hay, an ox, and a donkey into this rocky cave!
stops.saintQuote: “I want to do something that will recall to memory the Little Child who was born in Bethlehem, and to see with bodily eyes the inconveniences of His infant needs.”

detectiveClues.clueText: Look halfway between Assisi and Rome in the Sabine Mountains of Rieti Province. Called the "Franciscan Bethlehem," this sanctuary clings like an eagle’s nest to a vertical limestone cliff.

detectiveClues.headline: The Birthplace of Every Christmas Nativity Scene on Earth (1223)
detectiveClues.clueText: Before Christmas Eve 1223 in this mountain cave, no one had ever set up a three-dimensional Christmas Nativity manger scene. Today the village hosts a permanent International Museum of the Nativity!

detectiveClues.headline: The Torchlit Woods, the Ox & Donkey, and the Deacon Singing the Gospel
detectiveClues.clueText: Inspired by his recent pilgrimage to the Holy Land, Francis had a hay-filled manger, an ox, and an ass brought into this rocky grotto on Christmas night 1223 and sang the Christmas Gospel in deacon’s vestments.

stops.title: The Sacred Mountain & The Chasm of the Stigmata
stops.subtitle: Ascend the beech-forested cliff of Mount La Verna in Tuscany
stops.eraLabel: September 14, 1224 AD · The Stigmata
stops.imageCaption: Franciscan Sanctuary of La Verna perched atop the sheer limestone cliff and ancient forest of Mount Penna in Chiusi della Verna, Tuscany, Italy.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today at the Sanctuary of La Verna (at 1,128 meters altitude in the Casentino Apennines of Arezzo Province, Tuscany, Italy), pilgrims walk through ancient beech forests, admire monumental glazed terracotta reliefs by Andrea della Robbia, and pray in the cliff-edge Chapel of the Stigmata.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Mount La Verna was gifted to St. Francis as a solitary retreat in 1213 by a Tuscan knight named Count Orlando of Chiusi—who wrote a parchment deed gifting the entire forested mountain peak "without any tax, in exchange only for the prayers of Brother Francis and his companions"!
stops.saintQuote: “You are beauty, You are meekness, You are our protector, You are our guardian and defender.”
stops.detectiveCaseTitle: Case #5 · The Cliff-Top Tuscan Sanctuary of the Six-Winged Seraph
stops.detectiveLeadPrompt: Read the 3 clues below, then spin the 3D Globe to the high Tuscan mountain peak where Francis received the Stigmata in 1224.

detectiveClues.headline: A 1,128-Meter Limestone Cliff Sanctuary in the Casentino Forests of Tuscany
detectiveClues.clueText: Look north of Umbria into eastern Tuscany (Province of Arezzo). Rising abruptly above a primeval forest of towering beech and silver fir trees is the sheer rock plateau of Mount Penna.

detectiveClues.headline: Andrea della Robbia’s Glazed Terracottas & The Daily 3 PM Procession
detectiveClues.clueText: Because winter frost destroys wall frescoes at this high altitude, the churches here house the world’s largest collection of weatherproof blue-and-white glazed terracotta masterpieces by Renaissance sculptor Andrea della Robbia!

detectiveClues.headline: The Forty-Day Fast of St. Michael & The Wounds of Christ (September 1224)
detectiveClues.clueText: Gifted this mountain by Count Orlando in 1213, Francis was keeping a 40-day fast on the cliff ledge around the Feast of the Exaltation of the Cross in 1224 when he beheld a six-winged seraph and received the Stigmata.

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The small stone chapel clinging to the lower rock ledge above the sheer chasm.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #1 on the lower cliff-edge chapel on the right.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: What Happened Here: The Stigmata on Mount La Verna (September 1224)
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Before dawn near the Feast of the Exaltation of the Cross in September 1224, while praying on this isolated rock ledge on Mount La Verna, Francis beheld a vision of a six-winged seraph and received the five wounds of Christ—the first recorded Stigmata in history.
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The cliff-edge ledge where St. Francis received the wounds of Christ in 1224

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The stone bell tower and basilica complex crowning the rock cliff.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #2 on the bell tower and main sanctuary buildings.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Did You Know? Count Orlando’s Gift & The Reliquary of Brother Leo’s Parchment
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Right after receiving the Stigmata on La Verna, Francis took a piece of parchment and wrote in his own hand the "Blessing for Brother Leo" (the famous Chartula)—signed with the Tau cross—which is still preserved today in Assisi!
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The handwritten parchment blessing Francis wrote for Brother Leo on Mount La Verna

stops.title: The Little Portion & Welcome Sister Death
stops.subtitle: Behold the tiny Portiuncula Chapel beneath the dome of Santa Maria degli Angeli
stops.eraLabel: October 3, 1226 AD · Cradle of the Order & Transitus
stops.imageCaption: The tiny 4th-century stone Chapel of the Portiuncula preserved directly beneath the great marble dome of the Papal Basilica of Santa Maria degli Angeli in the valley below Assisi.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Today in Santa Maria degli Angeli (on the valley floor 4 km below the hill of Assisi in Umbria, Italy), pilgrims walk inside the seventh-largest church in the world to find the tiny rough-stone Chapel of the Portiuncula ("Little Portion") and the Chapel of the Transitus where Francis died on October 3, 1226.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Because Benedictine monks owned the tiny woodland chapel of the Portiuncula, Francis insisted on never owning the property outright—so every year he sent the monks a basket of small river fish (lasche) as annual rent, a tradition still reenacted every August 2 during the Pardon of Assisi!
stops.saintQuote: “Praised be You, my Lord, through our Sister Bodily Death, from whom no living person can escape.”

globePlacement.regionLabel: Umbrian Valley Plain, Santa Maria degli Angeli, Italy

stops.detectiveCaseTitle: Case #6 · The Tiny Stone Chapel Inside a Giant Marble Dome
stops.detectiveLeadPrompt: Read the 3 clues below, then spin the 3D Globe to the Umbrian valley town below Assisi where the tiny Portiuncula chapel is enclosed inside a massive Papal Basilica.

detectiveClues.headline: A Valley Town Directly Below Assisi Housing the 7th-Largest Basilica on Earth
detectiveClues.clueText: Look to the flat Umbrian valley plain just 4 km southwest of Assisi’s hill, right beside the Assisi train station. In 1569, Pope Pius V ordered a monumental domed basilica built around a tiny 4th-century chapel.

detectiveClues.headline: Rent Paid with a Basket of River Fish & The Thornless Rose Garden
detectiveClues.clueText: Inside this basilica stands a stone chapel only 4 meters wide, rented from Benedictine monks for an annual basket of river fish, alongside a courtyard garden where ancient rose bushes grow completely without thorns!

detectiveClues.headline: "Welcome, Sister Death!" (October 3, 1226)
detectiveClues.clueText: This tiny chapel ("The Little Portion") was the motherhouse of the Franciscan movement, where Clare received her habit and where Francis asked to be laid on the bare earth at sunset on October 3, 1226.

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The golden frescoed gable of the tiny stone Portiuncula chapel in the center.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #1 on the tiny stone chapel beneath the dome.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: What Happened Here: The "Little Portion" & The Pardon of Assisi
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Repaired by St. Francis’s own hands in 1208, this tiny stone chapel—the Portiuncula ("Little Portion")—became the cradle of the Franciscan Order, where the first friars gathered, where St. Clare took her vows on Palm Sunday 1212, and where Francis obtained the famous Portiuncula Indulgence ("Pardon of Assisi") in 1216.
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The tiny stone chapel where Francis founded the Order of Friars Minor

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The small stone doorway of the Chapel of the Transitus on the left.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #2 on the rustic stone wall and doorway on the left.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Did You Know? Laid on the Bare Earth to Welcome "Sister Death" (1226)
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Just steps from the Portiuncula stands the tiny infirmary cell—now the Chapel of the Transitus—where on the evening of October 3, 1226, 44-year-old Francis asked to be laid on the bare ground, sang Psalm 142, and welcomed "Sister Bodily Death." Inside rests the actual rough wool cord he wore!
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The infirmary cell beside the Portiuncula where St. Francis died on October 3, 1226

hiddenArtifacts.riddleToFind: The soaring white marble dome rising directly overhead.
hiddenArtifacts.hintDirection: Click marker #3 on the great white cupola dome at the top.
hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: Where Is It Modern Day Now? Basilica of Santa Maria degli Angeli, Assisi, Italy
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Today in Santa Maria degli Angeli (4 km below Assisi in Umbria, Italy), Galeazzo Alessi’s soaring 16th-century Papal Basilica shelters both the Portiuncula and the Chapel of the Transitus, plus the garden where white doves still nest in the hands of Francis’s statue!
hiddenArtifacts.stoneKeyMeaning: The Papal Basilica in the valley below Assisi enclosing the Portiuncula today

detectiveClues.headline: Martyr of Charity in New Orleans Yellow Fever
detectiveClues.clueText: Appointed pastor of **St. Mary’s Assumption Church** in **New Orleans** in **1866**, Fr. Seelos quickly won the whole city’s heart—ministering joyfully to German, Irish, French, and African-American parishioners alike. Seelos walked tirelessly house to house day and night nursing the dying until he caught the fever himself and died smiling on **October 4, 1867**, at age **48!**

stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Visit the peaceful **Monastery of Prouilhe** overlooking the sunlit hills of Occitanie, where Dominican nuns have kept the gentle rhythm of contemplative prayer alive for over eight centuries!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Wait—what does the word **"Rosary"** literally mean?! It comes from the Latin ***rosarium***—**"a crown or garden of roses"**—because every single Hail Mary prayed with love is like placing a fresh blooming rose into Mary’s hands!

Bartolo Longo**—who had dabbled in dark occultism before returning wholeheartedly to Christ—walked through the impoverished, bandit-ridden **Valley of Pompeii** feeling hopeless until a clear inner voice whispered: **"Spread the Rosary, and you will be saved!"** Starting with a tattered painting rescued in a horse-cart of manure, Longo built the dazzling **Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary of Pompeii**—plus **schools and homes for the children of prison inmates**, transforming a forgotten wasteland into a gleaming city of mercy!

stops.title: Staying Through Famine at El-Obeid & Legacy Across Continents
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across El-Obeid, Kordofan to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: 1873 – 1881 · El-Obeid, Kordofan, Sudan
stops.imageCaption: Golden ochre acacia savanna stretching beneath a vast amber Sudanese twilight sky where a gentle white-bearded bishop shares water and grain beside a mud-brick schoolhouse.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Canonized in **2003**, **St. Daniel Comboni’s** prophetic last words came blazingly true: over **3,000 Comboni Missionaries**—priests, brothers, sisters, and lay volunteers from Africa, Latin America, Asia, and Europe—now serve the poorest communities in over **40 countries worldwide!**
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: St. Daniel Comboni famously called Africa ***"the poorest and most abandoned jewel of humanity"***—and insisted that true missionaries must *"make common cause"* with the people they serve in joyful solidarity!
stops.saintQuote: I am dying, but my work will not die—Africa will rise in light!

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Deep inland in the savanna oasis of **El-Obeid**, Comboni founded joyful model villages of freed families—teaching carpentry, farming, literacy, and medicine! When catastrophic **drought, locusts, and famine** struck Sudan in **1878–1881**, friends urged the exhausted 50-year-old bishop to sail back to Italy to recover. Comboni refused to abandon his flock—giving away his last bread until he died peacefully in **Khartoum on October 10, 1881**, whispering: **"I am dying, but my work will NOT die!"**

stops.title: Chosen Among the Seven Deacons in Jerusalem
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Hierosolyma & Sebaste (Samaria) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: c. 33 – 35 AD · Jerusalem & Ancient Samaria
stops.imageCaption: Warm golden sunlight filling a first-century limestone courtyard in Jerusalem where a smiling young Greek-speaking deacon distributes loaves of bread and olive oil to grateful widows.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: From the ancient stones of **Jerusalem** to the terraced hills of **Sebaste (Samaria)**, Philip’s leap over old ethnic grudges marks the very moment the Gospel burst beyond borders.
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: St. Philip is the **ONLY** person in the entire New Testament explicitly given the title **"The Evangelist"** (Acts 21:8)—showing that practical table-service and bold storytelling go hand in hand!
stops.saintQuote: Go up and walk right beside that chariot—no seeker is ever too far away!

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Don’t confuse him with Philip the Apostle! stops.eraLabel: c. 35 AD · Desert Road From Jerusalem Toward Gaza
stops.ancientPlaceName: Via Maris / Desert Road to Gaza (Ein Haniya)
stops.imageCaption: Sunlit limestone desert highway winding past a bubbling clear spring oasis where an eager deacon jogs beside an ornate wooden chariot reading an open Isaiah scroll.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Near Jerusalem’s Refaim Valley, archaeologists uncovered ancient Byzantine baptismal pools at **Ein Haniya**—long venerated by early pilgrims as **"Philip’s Fountain,"** where Christianity first began its journey into Africa!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: That single roadside conversation in Acts 8 made the **Ethiopian Treasurer** the **very first documented Gentile and African convert to Christ**—long before St. Paul ever sailed to Europe!
stops.saintQuote: Look, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?

hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Wait—picture one of the greatest road-trip scenes in the whole Bible (**Acts 8**)! Guided by an angel onto the quiet southern road toward **Gaza**, Philip spotted the royal Treasurer of **Queen Candace of Ethiopia** riding home in his chariot reading the **Prophet Isaiah** aloud! Jogging right alongside the rolling wheels, Philip asked warmly: **"Do you understand what you are reading?"** Climbing aboard, he explained Jesus from Isaiah 53 until the thrilled official spotted roadside water and cried: **"Look, here is water! What is to stop me from being baptized?!"**

stops.title: A Discouraged Apostle Beside the Ebro River (40 AD)
stops.subtitle: Sweep your lantern across Caesaraugusta (Roman Zaragoza) to uncover 3 hidden memories
stops.eraLabel: January 2, 40 AD · Banks of the Ebro River, Zaragoza, Spain
stops.imageCaption: Warm starlit golden glow along the banks of Spain’s wide Ebro River where a weary bearded apostle kneels in wonder before a radiant luminous woman standing atop a tall jasper stone pillar.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Standing inside the **Holy Chapel of Zaragoza**, pilgrims can literally reach through an oval opening in the marble wall to kiss the **original smooth 2,000-year-old jasper pillar** worn glossy by millions of loving hands!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: That 40 AD chapel built beside the Ebro by St. James is cherished across Christendom as the **very first church in world history dedicated to the Virgin Mary!**
stops.saintQuote: Take heart—even when your work seems small, God’s promise stands firm as a pillar of stone!

hiddenArtifacts.foundTitle: A Discouraged Apostle Beside the Ebro River (40 AD)
hiddenArtifacts.storyUnlocked: Even mighty apostles get discouraged! According to Spain’s oldest Christian tradition, in the year **40 AD**, **St. James the Greater** had trekked all the way to Roman Hispania (**Caesaraugusta**, modern Zaragoza) and felt heartbroken because barely eight locals had listened to his preaching! Praying sadly beside the dark rushing **Ebro River** on the night of **January 2, 40 AD**, he heard soft singing—and beheld **the Virgin Mary** (still living in Jerusalem, appearing in bilocation!) standing radiantly atop a gleaming **pillar of jasper**, promising: **"This place shall stand firm as a pillar of faith until the end of time!"**

According to Spain’s oldest Christian tradition, in the year **40 AD**, **St. James the Greater** had trekked all the way to Roman Hispania (**Caesaraugusta**, modern Zaragoza) and felt heartbroken because barely eight locals had listened to his preaching! detectiveClues.clueText: Here is why millions owe **St. Peter of Alcántara** a huge thank-you! Around **1560**, when skeptical theologians accused **St. Teresa of Ávila** of hallucinating and tried to block her dream of founding tiny joyful Carmelite convents, Teresa was terrified and nearly gave up! stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Visit the dazzling **Basilica of St. Emmeram in Regensburg**—where **St. Wolfgang’s** ancient stone crypt has welcomed grateful Bavarians and Bohemians for over **1,030 years!**

stops.eraLabel: c. 976 – 994 · St. Wolfgang im Salzkammergut, Austria
stops.imageCaption: Mirror-clear turquoise Alpine Austrian lake surrounded by soaring forested mountain peaks and a charming white-steepled lakeside church glowing in crisp autumn sunset light.
stops.whatYouCanSeeToday: Step inside the picturesque **Pilgrimage Church of St. Wolfgang** right on the emerald shore of **Lake Wolfgangsee** to marvel at **Michael Pacher’s** breathtaking 1481 gilded winged altarpiece—a crowning jewel of Alpine sacred art!
stops.didYouKnowHighlight: Dying peacefully while traveling down the Danube at **Pupping** on **October 31, 994**, St. Wolfgang asked simply for the chapel doors to be left **wide open** so every poor neighbor could walk right in and pray beside him!
stops.saintQuote: Leave the doors wide open—a shepherd belongs to his people until his very last breath.
